\chapter{Please}
\label{ch:fr-please}
\hlchaptermodality{19}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say please in French and choose between s'il vous plaît and s'il te plaît depending on who I am speaking to.}

Say s'il vous plaît with its silent final -t, take it apart into 'if it pleases you', then switch to s'il te plaît for a friend. The chapter's only lesson, so the payoff covers everything it introduces.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[s'il vous plaît]{s'il vous plaît — please}

\label{lesson:FR-C19-sil-vous-plait}



\begin{quote}
French doesn't order you to do things — it asks, very politely, \emph{if it would please you.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{s'il vous plaît} = \textbf{please} — but taken apart it's a tiny sentence:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{s'} (\emph{si}, \textquotedblleft{}if\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{il} (\textquotedblleft{}it\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{vous} (\textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{plaît} (\textquotedblleft{}pleases\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{if it pleases you.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

You're not demanding; you're checking whether the favour would please them. It's the polite indirectness Spanish also uses in \emph{por favor} (\textquotedblleft{}for a favour\textquotedblright{}) — same courtesy, built a different way.

The verb \textbf{plaît} is from Latin \textbf{placēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to please\textquotedblright{} — which English borrowed wholesale: \textbf{please}, \textbf{pleasure}, \textbf{pleasant}, and (via \textquotedblleft{}calm, pleasing\textquotedblright{}) even \textbf{placid}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Formal and familiar}]
French chooses the word for \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} by who you're talking to — and \emph{please} comes in both:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{s'il vous plaît} — \emph{vous}, the \textbf{formal / plural} you (a stranger, an elder, a room). Often written \textbf{SVP}.
  \item \textbf{s'il te plaît} — \emph{te}, the \textbf{familiar} you (a friend, a child).
\end{itemize}

Two sounds to respect: the final \textbf{‑t} of \emph{plaît} is \textbf{silent} (\emph{pleh}), and \emph{plaît} itself carries the \emph{ai} = \emph{eh} you've met.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}s'il vous plaît\textquotedblright{} — final t silent, \emph{see voo pleh}
  \item taken apart — \textquotedblleft{}if it pleases you\textquotedblright{}
  \item familiar — \textquotedblleft{}s'il te plaît\textquotedblright{} to a friend
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say please in French? (\textbf{s'il vous plaît}.) What does it literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{If it pleases you.}\textquotedblright{}) Which Latin verb is \emph{plaît} from, and what English words come from it? (\textbf{placēre} — \emph{please, pleasure, placid}.) When do you say \textbf{s'il te plaît} instead? (To someone you address as \textbf{tu} — a friend or child.)
\end{tcolorbox}
